summary: Provides information and requirements for how WebRTC implementations should use Forward Error Correction (FEC), which sends extra data so receivers can recover lost packets without asking for retransmission. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If you send a message with a few extra clues, the reader can fill in a word that got smudged without asking you to repeat it. This document says how video-call software should use such extra clues.

subtitle: Which error-correction tricks WebRTC audio and video should use to survive lost packets, and when to turn them on.

tldr.problem: When packet loss is high or perfect media quality is essential, WebRTC needs a way to recover lost packets proactively, but there are several FEC mechanisms and they suit different media.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares three kinds of FEC (a separate FEC stream, redundant encoding, and codec-specific in-band FEC), recommends one per media type, says how to signal support in SDP, and tells implementations to use FEC adaptively.
tldr.outcome: Audio should use redundant encoding or the codec's built-in FEC, and video should use a separate Flexible FEC stream. Implementations MUST be able to receive and use the FEC formats for their supported audio codecs. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8854 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. The unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why WebRTC Needs FEC Guidance
sections.content:
In situations where packet loss is high, or perfect media quality is essential, Forward Error Correction (FEC) can be used to proactively recover from packet losses. FEC means sending redundant information in an outgoing packet stream so that data can still be recovered even if some packets are lost.

There are several ways to do this for RTP media streams (RFC 3550). This RFC provides guidance on which FEC mechanisms WebRTC implementations should use, and how to use them. It covers audio, video and application data, plus when to switch FEC on.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a lot of the little pieces of a video call get lost on the way. Sending a few extra pieces ahead of time lets the receiver patch the holes without waiting.

sections.title: Three Kinds of FEC
sections.content:
The RFC lists three mechanisms and their trade-offs.

A separate FEC stream (from RFC 5956) sends FEC packets as an independent RTP stream with its own SSRC and payload type, multiplexed with the primary encoding. One FEC packet can protect several primary packets, but each FEC packet has its own IP/UDP/RTP/FEC header, and that overhead can be excessive, for example when every primary packet gets its own FEC packet. It can recover whole RTP packets, including the full RTP header.

Redundant encoding (RFC 2198) piggybacks redundant data on an existing packet. The copy may be exact, or a smaller, lower-quality version for variable-bitrate codecs, and it can cover several prior audio frames. There is only one set of headers, so it is efficient, but only when everything fits in one packet (less than an MTU). It is therefore generally not useful for video. It cannot recover the marker bit, CSRC information or header extensions.

Codec-specific in-band FEC is built into some audio codecs, notably Opus and AMR. It adds no extra framing, so it can be slightly more efficient than redundant encoding, but it cannot recover any of the RTP header.

For Opus, important frames are re-encoded at a lower bitrate and appended to the next payload. The RFC says experiments indicate an overhead of only about 20-30%. Opus FEC carries redundancy only for the immediately preceding frame, so several consecutive lost packets cannot be fully recovered, which can be a problem on wireless networks.

For AMR and AMR-Wideband, packets can contain copies or lower-quality encodings of multiple prior audio frames.
sections.eli5: You can mail a spare copy of a page in its own envelope, tuck a smaller copy inside the next envelope, or have the writer build hints into the page itself. Each way costs a different amount of extra paper.

sections.title: FEC for Audio
sections.content:
For audio the RFC makes these recommendations:

  • Variable-bitrate codecs without internal FEC: redundant encoding with lower-fidelity versions of the previous packets is RECOMMENDED, because the redundant copies can be much smaller than the primary encoding.
  • Opus: the built-in Opus FEC is RECOMMENDED. It gives single-frame redundancy only, so if multi-packet protection is needed, redundant encoding with reduced-bitrate Opus encodings SHOULD be used instead.
  • AMR and AMR-WB: their built-in FEC is RECOMMENDED, as it is slightly more efficient than redundant encoding.
  • Constant-bitrate codecs such as PCMU: redundant encoding MAY be used, but the bitrate increase can be significant, and suddenly raising bitrate to cope with congestion losses may make things worse.
  • A separate FEC stream is NOT RECOMMENDED for audio, since the low packet rate (usually one packet per frame) makes its overhead higher than the other options.

These mechanisms cannot recover parts of the RTP header, such as CSRCs and header extensions like those in RFC 6464 and RFC 6465. Implementations SHOULD account for this and try to approximate that information.
sections.eli5: For voice, the best plan is usually to let the voice recorder add its own small backup copies. A whole extra stream of backups would cost more than the tiny voice pieces are worth.

sections.title: Signaling FEC Support in SDP
sections.content:
Support is negotiated with the SDP offer/answer model (RFC 3264).

For audio, support for redundant encoding SHOULD be indicated by listing audio/red as an extra media type in the "m=" section of the offer. An answerer can reject it by leaving audio/red out of its answer. Codec-specific FEC is typically indicated through a=fmtp parameters.

  • Opus: a receiver MUST indicate it is ready to use incoming FEC with useinbandfec=1. The parameter is declarative and can be negotiated separately for each media direction.
  • AMR and AMR-WB: redundant encoding support and maximum depth are controlled by the max-red parameter. Receivers MUST include it and set it to an appropriate value.

For video, support for an SSRC-multiplexed Flexible FEC stream SHOULD be indicated by adding video/flexfec to the offer's "m=" section. Answerers can reject it by omitting that media type. FEC-only "m=" lines and the SDP grouping mechanism from RFC 5956 are not currently defined for WebRTC, SHOULD NOT be offered, and SHOULD be rejected by answerers unless they know how to handle them.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side says which kinds of backup it understands. If one side does not know a kind, it simply does not list it and the other side skips it.

sections.title: FEC for Video and Application Data
sections.content:
Video frames often need several RTP packets because of their size. A separate FEC stream can protect many packets with one FEC packet. The Flexible FEC mechanism in RFC 8627 can also protect multiple RTP streams with one FEC stream, including every stream in a BUNDLE group. For video, a separate FEC stream using the Flexible FEC RTP payload format is therefore RECOMMENDED.

The receiver demultiplexes the FEC stream by SSRC, then matches it to the primary stream(s) using the CSRC(s) in the RTP header of Flexible FEC repair packets, or the SSRC field in the FEC header of retransmission packets. When BUNDLE is used, only one Flexible FEC repair stream is created per BUNDLE group, even if Flexible FEC is negotiated for each primary stream.

For application data, WebRTC data channels (RFC 8831) already provide transport-level retransmission with full and partial reliability. Because the application controls exactly what it sends, it can monitor packet statistics and do its own FEC. The RFC therefore makes no FEC recommendation for the underlying data transport.
sections.eli5: A video frame is big and comes in many pieces, so one backup piece can cover several of them. For plain app messages, the app can build its own backups, so this document stays out of it.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content:
Implementations MUST be able to receive and make use of the relevant FEC formats for the audio codecs they support, and MUST indicate this support as described for audio. Using these formats when sending is RECOMMENDED.

The general FEC mechanism in RFC 8627 SHOULD also be supported. Implementations MAY support additional FEC mechanisms, for example RFC 5109.
sections.eli5: Every device must be able to read the backup hints for the voices it understands. Sending backups is encouraged, and other kinds of backups are allowed if a device wants them.

sections.title: Using FEC Adaptively
sections.content:
FEC always sends redundant data, and the total must stay within the limits set by congestion control and the receiver. That leaves less bandwidth for the primary encoding even when the redundant data is never used. Methods such as RTX (RFC 4588) or Flexible FEC's retransmission mode send redundant data only when needed, at the cost of an extra round trip and more media latency.

So WebRTC implementations SHOULD prefer RTX or Flexible FEC retransmissions when the connection RTT is within the application's latency budget. Otherwise they SHOULD send only as much FEC as the observed packet loss requires (for example, judged from RTCP receiver reports), unless the application is willing to pay a quality penalty to avoid losses proactively.

  • When probing bandwidth, FEC data SHOULD be used as the extra data, since extra data is being sent anyway.
  • With layered codecs where only base layer frames are critical to later decoding, FEC SHOULD be applied only to those base layer frames.

If loss is caused by network congestion, the extra bandwidth used by redundant data may make things worse and can lead to significant degradation of the network.
sections.eli5: Sending spare copies uses up road space. If the road is jammed, more cars make the jam worse, so only send as many spares as you really need.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In WebRTC, FEC only recovers data from lost packets. Corrupted packets are discarded by SRTP decryption. As described in RFC 3711, the default processing is FEC followed by SRTP at the sender, and SRTP followed by FEC at the receiver. This ordering is used for all the SRTP protection profiles used in DTLS-SRTP.

Security considerations for each individual FEC mechanism are in their own documents. The RFC requires no actions from IANA.
sections.eli5: The lock goes on after the backups are made and comes off before they are used, so the backups are protected too.
